preamble: The voiced lateral fricative can lose its laterality and become the central dental fricative [ð]. The clearest case is the Arabic letter ḍād: Classical Arabic ض is reconstructed as a pharyngealized voiced lateral fricative [ɮˤ] (or affricate), and in many vernaculars, notably Bedouin, Najdi, Gulf, Mesopotamian, Tunisian and Ḥassāniyya Arabic, it delateralized to [ðˤ], merging with ẓāʾ ظ. Pharyngealization is kept throughout; only the lateral release is lost.

examples.note: ض is mostly pronounced [ðˤ], identical to ظ.

examples.from: Classical Arabic ضلّ ḍalla [ɮˤalla] 'he went astray'
examples.note: Homophonous with ظلّ ḏ̣al 'shade', since ḍād and ẓāʾ have merged as [ðˤ].

sources: Versteegh, K. (1997). The Arabic Language. Edinburgh University Press, p. 89. https://edinburghuniversitypress.com/book-the-arabic-language-435.html
